```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
HAS_GLMNET <- requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)
HAS_CUDA <- isTRUE(rcupp::cuda_available())
RUN <- HAS_GLMNET && HAS_CUDA
```

```{r status, echo = FALSE}
if (!RUN) {
  cat("Live benchmark skipped: needs glmnet and a CUDA backend.\n")
}
```

This vignette measures the wall time of a Gaussian lasso lambda path fitted
by `glmnet` and by `cuda_glmnet()`. It reports the numbers as measured,
including the cases where `glmnet` is faster. A separate section then shows
where the compiled FISTA primitive is faster: against the package's own
pure-R reference solver, the baseline used by the companion benchmark. The
two baselines differ, so the two sections answer different questions. The
positive result is genuine but scoped, and it does not isolate the GPU
backend: it is a win for a compiled solver (built here with CUDA) over
interpreted R on large single solves, not a win over `glmnet`.

Two rules keep the comparison fair:

1. Both solvers get the **same explicit lambda grid**. `glmnet()` stops its
   default path early (on the companion example it fitted 15 of 20 planned
   values), so letting each build its own path would time different amounts
   of work.
2. Before timing, the coefficients at a mid-path lambda are compared. If
   they disagreed, the two solvers would not be doing comparable work. The
   `glmnet-comparison` vignette establishes that they agree.

Only the CUDA backend is timed. On a machine without a CUDA toolkit `rcupp`
builds a CPU reference shim; those timings are not representative of the GPU
path and are deliberately excluded. The live chunk is therefore guarded by
`requireNamespace("glmnet")` and `rcupp::cuda_available()`.

## Method

- One synthetic dataset per configuration, `n x p`, with five planted
  nonzero coefficients and Gaussian noise.
- A shared 30-value log-spaced grid from `lambda.max` down to
  `lambda.max * 1e-3`, where `lambda.max` follows the common `1/(2n)`
  convention after removing column means and scaling columns to unit
  population variance.
- Default model settings on both sides: `standardize = TRUE`,
  `intercept = TRUE`. `glmnet` uses its default `thresh`, `cuda_glmnet()`
  its default `tol = 1e-6`.
- One warm-up call per timed function (inside `time_median()`), then the
  median elapsed time of three repetitions via `system.time()`. The
  `gpu-vs-oracle` live chunk also runs ten `rcupp::lasso_fista()` calls to
  warm the GPU device before measuring; the static 2026-11-18 snapshots
  below were taken without that device warm-up, so the live chunk will not
  reproduce them exactly.
- Three variants: `glmnet`, `cuda_glmnet()` cold start (the default), and
  `cuda_glmnet(warm_start = TRUE)`.

## Reference measurement

Measured 2026-11-18 on a machine with an NVIDIA RTX 4070 Laptop GPU (8 GB),
CUDA Toolkit 13.1, R 4.6.1, glmnet 5.2 and cudaGlmnet 0.0.0.9002 (GPU
backend). Wall times in seconds; `cuda / glmnet` is how many times slower
the cold-start GPU path is.

| n | p | lambdas | glmnet (s) | cudaGlmnet (s) | warm_start (s) | cuda / glmnet | max coef diff |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | 50 | 30 | 0.002 | 0.568 | 0.363 | 284.0x | 1.0e-05 |
| 1000 | 100 | 30 | 0.003 | 0.357 | 0.254 | 119.0x | 6.6e-06 |
| 2000 | 200 | 30 | 0.012 | 0.448 | 0.278 | 37.3x | 1.1e-06 |
| 5000 | 200 | 30 | 0.037 | 0.318 | 0.263 | 8.6x | 8.7e-07 |

These are a snapshot, not a performance guarantee: they depend on the GPU,
the CUDA toolkit and the package versions. The chunk below regenerates them
on any machine with a CUDA backend.

## Reproduce the benchmark

```{r benchmark, eval = RUN}
make_data <- function(n, p) {
  set.seed(42)
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  beta <- rep(0, p)
  beta[1:5] <- c(2, -1.5, 1, -0.5, 0.75)
  list(X = X, y = drop(X %*% beta) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5))
}

common_lambda <- function(X, y, nlambda = 30L) {
  Xc <- X - matrix(colMeans(X), nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE)
  xs <- sqrt(colMeans(Xc^2))
  Xs <- Xc / matrix(xs, nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE)
  lmax <- max(abs(crossprod(Xs, y - mean(y)))) / nrow(X)
  exp(seq(log(lmax), log(lmax * 1e-3), length.out = nlambda))
}

time_median <- function(f, reps = 3L) {
  f()
  median(replicate(reps, system.time(f())[["elapsed"]]))
}

configs <- data.frame(n = c(200L, 1000L, 2000L, 5000L),
                      p = c(50L, 100L, 200L, 200L))

rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(configs)), function(i) {
  d <- make_data(configs$n[i], configs$p[i])
  lam <- common_lambda(d$X, d$y)

  j <- length(lam) %/% 2L
  g0 <- glmnet::glmnet(d$X, d$y, lambda = lam)
  c0 <- cuda_glmnet(d$X, d$y, lambda = lam)
  b_g <- as.matrix(stats::coef(g0, s = lam[j]))
  b_c <- coef(c0, s = lam[j])
  max_diff <- max(abs(b_g - b_c))
  stopifnot(max_diff < 1e-3)

  t_g <- time_median(function() glmnet::glmnet(d$X, d$y, lambda = lam))
  t_c <- time_median(function() cuda_glmnet(d$X, d$y, lambda = lam))
  t_w <- time_median(function() {
    cuda_glmnet(d$X, d$y, lambda = lam, warm_start = TRUE)
  })

  data.frame(n = configs$n[i], p = configs$p[i], lambdas = length(lam),
             glmnet_s = sprintf("%.3f", t_g),
             cuda_s = sprintf("%.3f", t_c),
             cuda_warm_s = sprintf("%.3f", t_w),
             cuda_over_glmnet = sprintf("%.1fx", t_c / t_g),
             max_coef_diff = sprintf("%.1e", max_diff))
})

knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, rows),
             caption = "Wall time (median of 3) for one 30-lambda path.")
```

## Interpreting the numbers

`glmnet` is faster across every configuration tested. Its Gaussian path is
solved by coordinate descent in a single compiled call, with warm starts
along the path: the number of passes per lambda falls steeply as the penalty
decreases. `cuda_glmnet()` instead runs one FISTA solve per lambda. By
default each is a cold start, including a power iteration for the Lipschitz
constant, plus an R-to-C++ call and R-level bookkeeping (coefficient
assembly and `dev.ratio`) for every lambda. At these matrix sizes GPU
throughput never makes up for that overhead.

`warm_start = TRUE` cuts the path time by roughly a third, since the cached
Lipschitz constant and the previous solution are reused. It is the better
setting for a full path, though still slower than `glmnet` here.

The gap narrows when the dense work per solve grows. On a single low-level
solve with no path bookkeeping (`rcupp::lasso_fista()` against `glmnet()` at
one lambda), `n = 5000, p = 1000` measured 0.073 s for the GPU solver
against 0.058 s for `glmnet`. The persistent session in `cuda_glmnet()` also
keeps the design matrix resident on the device for the whole path, which
removes repeated uploads across many fits.

The honest conclusion for these workloads: `glmnet` is the faster choice for
whole lambda paths. `cudaGlmnet` is a fixed-operator GPU FISTA bridge with a
persistent-device session, not yet a faster drop-in replacement for
`glmnet`'s path algorithm. This vignette is a measurement, not a performance
claim.

The next section changes the baseline and shows where the compiled FISTA
primitive is faster: against a pure-R implementation of the same algorithm.

## Compiled FISTA vs pure-R (large single solves)

**Result up front.** On one large fixed-lambda solve, `rcupp::lasso_fista()`
(a compiled primitive, built here with the CUDA backend) is several times
faster than `lasso_fista_cpu()`, the same algorithm written in pure R,
ranging from about 1.6x to about 26x across the four configurations in the
snapshot below. This is the workload the backend is built for: one big dense
solve with no per-lambda R-level bookkeeping. Two caveats frame the number.
First, the baseline is the pure-R reference solver, not `glmnet`. Second,
the comparison does not isolate the GPU: it is compiled code against
interpreted R, so both compilation and the CUDA backend contribute. A
separate check that ran the same comparison against a build of `rcupp` with
the CPU fallback (compiled, no CUDA) still beat pure R, by roughly
1.7x-2.1x on these sizes, so the larger CUDA figures combine a compilation
win with a backend win rather than measuring GPU acceleration alone.

The comparison above is deliberately hard: `glmnet` solves the whole path
with compiled Fortran coordinate descent. `cudaGlmnet` also ships
`lasso_fista_cpu()`, a pure-R FISTA reference with the identical numerical
contract (same objective, same power iteration for the Lipschitz constant,
same FISTA loop). It exists to verify the compiled path and was the baseline
of the companion benchmark. Against an interpreted implementation of the
same algorithm the compiled primitive wins, but the exact ratio is noisy and
does not reliably grow with problem size.

Measured 2026-11-18 on the same machine with the older protocol, before the
GPU device warm-up was added to the live chunk. The setup differs from
`Method` above: a single fixed lambda (`0.1 * lambda.max`) with columns
scaled to unit variance on the host before either solver runs, and
`tol = 1e-6` on both sides. Because the live chunk now warms the device, it
will not reproduce these numbers exactly. Before timing, the two coefficient
vectors are compared; they agree to roughly 1e-16, so both solvers do the
same work.

| n | p | pure-R FISTA (s) | compiled FISTA (s) | speedup vs pure-R | max coef diff |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 500 | 0.075 | 0.046 | 1.6x | 4.4e-16 |
| 2000 | 1000 | 0.337 | 0.058 | 5.8x | 2.2e-16 |
| 5000 | 1000 | 1.118 | 0.060 | 18.6x | 4.4e-16 |
| 10000 | 1000 | 2.851 | 0.110 | 25.9x | 4.4e-16 |

```{r speedup-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
nn <- c(1000L, 2000L, 5000L, 10000L)
pp <- c(500L, 1000L, 1000L, 1000L)
speedups <- c(1.6, 5.8, 18.6, 25.9)
m <- nn * pp / 1e6
plot(m, speedups, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Matrix size (n x p, millions of entries)",
     ylab = "Speedup vs pure-R FISTA (x)",
     main = "Speedup over pure-R FISTA (one snapshot)")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

The dashed line marks parity (1x). The four snapshot points sit above it,
but the ratio is noisy: other runs include values near or below 1x and the
curve need not rise steadily with size. The figure plots the static snapshot
above, so it renders even when the live benchmark is skipped.

Read the ratio against the right baseline: it says `rcupp::lasso_fista()`
(a compiled primitive built here with CUDA) is up to 26x faster than a
pure-R implementation of the same FISTA in this snapshot, not that it is
faster than `glmnet`, and not that the GPU backend alone accounts for the
gap. `glmnet` remains the faster choice for end-to-end Gaussian lasso paths,
as the table earlier in this vignette shows.

### Reading the timings honestly

These are snapshots, not guarantees. On a laptop, and on WSL in particular,
GPU wall time depends strongly on warm-up: a cold device runs at low clocks
and the first several solves are several times slower until the driver ramps
up. The live chunk below warms the device before timing for that reason.
Host load and the pure-R side vary too, so the exact speedup on any single
run can move by a wide margin; across repeated runs the same configuration
has ranged from below 1x to several tens of times faster. What is stable is
only the qualitative result: at large sizes a single dense solve is usually
several times faster with the compiled CUDA primitive than with the same
algorithm in interpreted R. The exact ratios, and whether they grow steadily
with size, are not stable. Treat the table as an illustrative measurement,
not a fixed number to quote as a benchmark.

```{r gpu-vs-oracle, eval = RUN}
# WSL/CUDA ramps GPU clocks lazily. Warm the device before timing so the
# numbers reflect steady state rather than the first cold solves.
set.seed(1)
Xw <- matrix(rnorm(600 * 60), 600, 60)
yw <- rnorm(600)
for (k in seq_len(10L)) {
  rcupp::lasso_fista(Xw, yw, lambda = 0.1, tol = 1e-6)
}

std_data <- function(X, y) {
  Xc <- X - matrix(colMeans(X), nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE)
  xs <- sqrt(colMeans(Xc^2))
  list(X = Xc / matrix(xs, nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE),
       y = y - mean(y))
}

oracle_configs <- data.frame(n = c(1000L, 2000L, 5000L, 10000L),
                             p = c(500L, 1000L, 1000L, 1000L))

oracle_rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(oracle_configs)), function(i) {
  d <- make_data(oracle_configs$n[i], oracle_configs$p[i])
  st <- std_data(d$X, d$y)
  lmax <- max(abs(crossprod(st$X, st$y))) / nrow(st$X)
  lam <- 0.1 * lmax

  b_r <- lasso_fista_cpu(st$X, st$y, lam, tol = 1e-6)$coefficients
  b_g <- rcupp::lasso_fista(st$X, st$y, lambda = lam, tol = 1e-6)$beta
  max_diff <- max(abs(b_r - b_g))
  stopifnot(max_diff < 1e-6)

  t_r <- time_median(function() {
    lasso_fista_cpu(st$X, st$y, lam, tol = 1e-6)
  })
  t_g <- time_median(function() {
    rcupp::lasso_fista(st$X, st$y, lambda = lam, tol = 1e-6)
  })

  data.frame(n = oracle_configs$n[i], p = oracle_configs$p[i],
             pure_r_s = sprintf("%.3f", t_r),
             gpu_s = sprintf("%.3f", t_g),
             gpu_speedup = sprintf("%.1fx", t_r / t_g),
             max_coef_diff = sprintf("%.1e", max_diff))
})

knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, oracle_rows),
             caption = "Single fixed-lambda solve: pure-R vs GPU FISTA.")
```

## Enabling the live benchmark

Both live chunks run only when `glmnet` is installed and
`rcupp::cuda_available()` is `TRUE`. The GPU chunk warms the device first, so
timings reflect steady state (see "Reading the timings honestly"). That
warm-up is newer than the static 2026-11-18 snapshots, so the live
single-solve numbers are a fresh measurement and will not reproduce the
table above exactly. CI runners have no CUDA Toolkit, so `rcupp` builds its
CPU reference shim there and the chunks are skipped; the reference tables
and the speedup figure above are static snapshots from a GPU machine. See
the CUDA build notes in the `gpu-lasso-comparison` vignette for how to link
the GPU backend.
